concepts.title: Normalization
concepts.summary: Storing each fact once, so updating it can't leave conflicting copies behind

variants.q: A `products` table stores `category_name` as text on every row. Marketing renames 'Shoes' to 'Footwear', and a week later some products still say 'Shoes'. What's the underlying problem?
choices: An update anomaly: one fact copied into many rows
A missing index on the `category_name` column
A lost update between two concurrent transactions
Replication lag on a read replica serving the page
variants.explain: The category name is a single fact stored in many places, so every copy has to be changed together. Normalising it into its own table means there's one row to update.

variants.q: Which design keeps exactly one copy of each category's name?
choices: A `category_name` column on `products` plus a check constraint
A `categories` table, referenced by `products.category_id`
A JSON array of category names stored on each product
A view selecting distinct `category_name` from `products`
variants.explain: With a foreign key, products point at one category row, and renaming touches that row only. The view still reads the duplicated copies underneath.

concepts.title: Storing money
concepts.summary: Using exact types (`numeric` or integer minor units) for money, never binary floating point

variants.q: Which Postgres column type is a poor choice for prices?
choices: `numeric(12,2)`
`bigint` holding cents
`double precision`
`integer` holding cents
variants.explain: Binary floating point can't represent most decimal fractions exactly, so sums drift by tiny amounts. `numeric` is exact decimal, and integer minor units are exact too.

variants.q: An invoice total is summed from three `0.10` line items in a `float` column, and the result is `0.30000000000000004`. Why?
choices: Postgres rounds floats on every insert
The transaction isolation level was wrong
The driver turned the value into a string
Binary floats can't hold 0.10 exactly
variants.explain: 0.10 has no exact binary representation, so each value is slightly off and the errors add up. Exact decimal or integer cents avoid it.

concepts.title: Surrogate vs natural keys
concepts.summary: Using a generated id as the primary key instead of a real-world value that can change

variants.q: `users.email` is the primary key, and six tables reference it. Users can change their email. What's the cost?
choices: Each email change must update all six tables
Text columns can't be indexed, so lookups get slow
A text primary key makes each insert lock the whole table
Foreign keys to a text column can't use `ON UPDATE CASCADE`
variants.explain: A primary key is copied into every referencing row, so changing it means changing all of them. A generated id never needs to change; email gets a unique constraint instead.

variants.q: A table's rows have a phone number that identifies them but can change. Which key design means a number change touches only one row?
choices: The phone number as primary key, with `ON UPDATE CASCADE` on references
A generated id as primary key, plus a unique constraint on the phone
No primary key, just a unique index on the phone number
A composite key of the phone number and the creation date
variants.explain: Other tables reference the stable id, so only the row's phone column changes. `ON UPDATE CASCADE` works, but it rewrites every referencing row.

concepts.title: Unique constraints with soft delete
concepts.summary: Keeping a value unique among live rows only, when deleted rows stay in the table

variants.q: Users are soft-deleted with `deleted_at`. An email must be unique among active users only, so a deleted user's email can sign up again. Which Postgres index does that?
choices: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users (email, deleted_at)`
`CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users (email)`
`CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`
`CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NOT NULL`
variants.explain: A partial unique index only covers active rows, so deleted rows don't block a new signup. A plain unique index on `email` would.

variants.q: Someone uses `UNIQUE (email, deleted_at)` instead. Two active users with the same email are inserted, both with `deleted_at` NULL. What happens by default in Postgres?
choices: The second insert fails with a unique violation
The second insert silently replaces the first row
Postgres won't create a constraint on a nullable column
Both inserts succeed: NULLs don't count as equal
variants.explain: In a unique constraint, NULL never equals NULL, so the pair never collides while rows are active. Postgres 15+ offers `NULLS NOT DISTINCT`, but the partial index is the usual fix.

concepts.title: timestamptz vs timestamp
concepts.summary: In Postgres, `timestamptz` stores an instant (UTC); `timestamp` stores a wall-clock time with no zone

variants.q: Servers in two time zones insert `now()` into a `timestamp` (without time zone) column, each session using its local `TimeZone`. What goes wrong?
choices: Each stores local wall time, so values can't be compared
Nothing: Postgres converts both values to UTC automatically
The insert fails, because `now()` returns a different type
The values are stored as text and sort alphabetically
variants.explain: Casting to `timestamp` drops the zone after converting to the session's local time, so the column mixes clocks. `timestamptz` stores the instant and compares correctly.

variants.q: A `timestamptz` value is inserted as `'2026-03-01 09:00+07'`. What does Postgres keep?
choices: The local `09:00` and the `+07` offset, both
The instant in UTC; the `+07` isn't kept
The local `09:00` only, dropping the offset
A text copy of exactly what was inserted
variants.explain: `timestamptz` normalises to UTC and displays in the session's zone; the original offset is gone. If you need the user's zone, store it in its own column.

concepts.title: Database constraints
concepts.summary: Enforcing invariants (CHECK, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE) in the database, where every code path hits them

variants.q: Stock must never go below zero. The order service checks this, but an admin script and a bulk import also update stock directly. What enforces the rule on every path?
choices: A comment on the column that describes the rule
A unit test for the order service's own check
A `CHECK (stock >= 0)` constraint on the table
An index on the `stock` column for fast reads
variants.explain: A constraint is checked on every write, whichever code sends it. Application checks only cover the paths that remember to call them.

variants.q: `order_items.order_id` references `orders.id` by convention only, with no foreign key. What can happen that a foreign key would prevent?
choices: Two items for the same product in one order
Orders whose total doesn't match their items
Slow joins between `orders` and `order_items`
Items pointing at orders that don't exist
variants.explain: A foreign key rejects references to missing rows. It doesn't speed up joins by itself; Postgres doesn't index the referencing column automatically.

skills.title: Query optimization
skills.summary: Finding slow queries, using indexes and reading query plans

concepts.title: Reading a query plan
concepts.summary: Using `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to see how a query actually ran: scans, joins, estimated vs actual rows

variants.q: In Postgres, what's the key difference between `EXPLAIN` and `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`?
choices: `ANALYZE` executes the query and shows real rows and timings
`ANALYZE` also refreshes the table's statistics
`ANALYZE` prints the plan as JSON instead of text
`ANALYZE` works only on `SELECT` statements
variants.explain: `EXPLAIN` shows the planner's estimates; `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs the query and adds what really happened, so wrap an `UPDATE` or `DELETE` in a transaction you roll back. Refreshing statistics is the separate `ANALYZE` command.

variants.q:
What does this plan suggest?

```
Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..41000.00 rows=12 width=64) (actual time=0.03..812.40 rows=9 loops=1)
  Filter: (customer_id = 42)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 1999991
```
choices: Most rows are dead, so the table needs `VACUUM`
The statistics are stale, since 12 estimated isn't 9
There's probably no usable index on `customer_id`
Nothing; a sequential scan is always the fastest
variants.explain: It read two million rows to return nine, filtering out the rest, which is what happens without an index on the filtered column. 'Rows Removed by Filter' counts rows that didn't match, not dead rows, and an estimate of 12 against 9 actual is accurate.

concepts.title: Composite index column order
concepts.summary: Which queries a multi-column index can serve depends on the order of its columns

variants.q:
Which single index serves this query best?

```sql
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE tenant_id = $1
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
```
choices: `(created_at, tenant_id)`
Separate indexes on each column
`(created_at)` on its own
`(tenant_id, created_at)`
variants.explain: With `tenant_id` first, the tenant's rows sit together already sorted by `created_at`, so Postgres reads 20 entries and stops. With `created_at` first, one tenant's rows are scattered through the index.

variants.q: For `WHERE status = 'open' AND created_at > now() - interval '1 day'`, which composite index is usually better?
choices: `(status, created_at)`: equality first, range second
`(created_at, status)`: the more selective column first
Either one: column order doesn't matter in a composite index
Neither: a B-tree can't serve a range condition
variants.explain: With the equality column first, matching rows form one contiguous range ordered by `created_at`. Range-first means scanning the whole day's range and filtering `status` inside it.

concepts.title: Sargable predicates
concepts.summary: Writing conditions the index can search, without wrapping the indexed column in a function

variants.q:
There's a B-tree index on `users(email)`. Why might this query not use it?

```sql
SELECT * FROM users WHERE lower(email) = 'a@b.com';
```
choices: B-tree indexes don't support text equality
The index holds `email`, not `lower(email)`
`lower()` takes a lock on the whole table
The planner never uses indexes for `SELECT *`
variants.explain: An index on a column only helps conditions on that column as stored. Add an expression index on `lower(email)`, or store emails lowercased.

variants.q: `created_at` (a `timestamptz`) is indexed. Which predicate for 'rows from 1 March 2026' can use the index as a range scan?
choices: `created_at::date = '2026-03-01'`
`date_trunc('day', created_at) = '2026-03-01'`
`created_at >= '2026-03-01' AND created_at < '2026-03-02'`
`to_char(created_at, 'YYYY-MM-DD') = '2026-03-01'`
variants.explain: Comparing the bare column with a range lets the index seek straight to it. The others compute a value from every row first, which the plain index can't help with.

concepts.title: Covering index (index-only scan)
concepts.summary: An index that holds every column a query needs, so the table itself isn't read

variants.q: `SELECT email FROM users WHERE tenant_id = $1` runs constantly on Postgres 11+. Which index lets Postgres answer it from the index alone?
choices: `CREATE INDEX ON users (email)`
`CREATE INDEX ON users (tenant_id)`
`CREATE INDEX ON users USING hash (tenant_id)`
`CREATE INDEX ON users (tenant_id) INCLUDE (email)`
variants.explain: `INCLUDE` stores `email` in the index entries without making it part of the key, so the query needs nothing from the table. With `(tenant_id)` alone, every match needs a table lookup for `email`.

variants.q: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows an *Index Only Scan* with a high `Heap Fetches` count. What's the likely cause?
choices: Pages aren't marked all-visible yet; VACUUM helps
The index is corrupt and needs a `REINDEX` to fix it
The query selects columns that the index doesn't hold
The table has no primary key, so rows can't be found
variants.explain: Postgres must check the table for rows on pages the visibility map doesn't mark all-visible. A recently vacuumed table needs few heap fetches.

concepts.title: Indexes (B-tree)
concepts.summary: A sorted structure that lets the database find matching rows without reading the whole table

variants.q: `SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1` takes 2 seconds on a 10-million-row table, and the plan shows a sequential scan. What's the usual fix?
choices: Add `LIMIT 1` so the scan stops at the first match
Increase the application's connection pool size
Run `VACUUM FULL` on the table
Create an index on `users(email)`
variants.explain: An index on `email` lets the database jump to the matching rows instead of reading all ten million. `LIMIT 1` can stop early, but on average it still reads a large share of the table.

variants.q: Why not simply add an index on every column of a busy, write-heavy table?
choices: Every insert and update must also update each index
Databases allow only one index per table
Reads get slower once a table has three indexes
Indexes are rebuilt from scratch every night
variants.explain: Each index is a separate structure that writes must keep in sync, so it costs write time and storage. Add the ones your queries actually use.

concepts.title: Stale planner statistics
concepts.summary: The planner picks plans from stored statistics; after big data changes, outdated stats give bad plans until `ANALYZE` runs

variants.q: A Postgres job bulk-loads millions of rows into a table, then immediately runs a large join on it. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows row estimates off from the actual counts by orders of magnitude, and a nested loop that runs for minutes. What's the most direct fix?
choices: Run `REINDEX` on the table's indexes
Run `ANALYZE` on the table after the load
Raise `max_connections` for the job
Add an index on every join column
variants.explain: The planner estimates rows from statistics gathered by `ANALYZE`; right after a big load they describe the old data, so it picks a plan suited to a much smaller table. Autovacuum would analyze it eventually, but not before the job's next statement.

variants.q: A Postgres query was fast for months, then started using a much slower plan. Nobody changed the code, the indexes or the settings. What's the most likely explanation?
choices: Postgres caches every plan until the server restarts
Indexes expire after a set age and stop being used
The planner picks at random among equal-cost plans
Plans come from statistics, and the data has shifted
variants.explain: The planner is cost-based: as row counts and value distributions change, its estimates change and a different plan can win, sometimes wrongly. Comparing estimated and actual rows in `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows where it went wrong.

skills.title: Transactions & consistency
skills.summary: Transactions, isolation levels and concurrent writes

concepts.title: Lost update
concepts.summary: Two read-modify-write transactions race, and one silently overwrites the other's change

choices: Postgres rejects the second `UPDATE` by itself
Both succeed, and the last unit is sold twice
Both fail with a deadlock error
The second waits, because `SELECT` locked the row
variants.explain: Both read stock 1, both pass the check, and both write 0. A plain `SELECT` takes no lock, and read committed doesn't detect the conflict.

variants.q: Which single statement removes the race from a read-check-write stock update?
choices: `UPDATE products SET stock = $3 WHERE id = $2`, after reading stock again
`SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = $2` inside `BEGIN ... COMMIT`
`UPDATE products SET stock = stock - $1 WHERE id = $2 AND stock >= $1`
`UPDATE products SET stock = GREATEST(stock - $1, 0) WHERE id = $2`
variants.explain: The check and the write happen atomically in one statement; if it affects 0 rows, the item is out of stock. `GREATEST` avoids negative stock but silently oversells.

variants.q: Many requests increment a counter row concurrently on Postgres's default isolation level. Which version never loses an increment?
choices: `SELECT n`, then `UPDATE counters SET n = $1` with `n + 1` computed in the app
The same `SELECT` and `UPDATE` pair, wrapped in `BEGIN ... COMMIT`
`UPDATE counters SET n = n + 1 WHERE id = $1`
Increment a counter in the app's memory and write it out every few seconds
variants.explain: The increment happens inside the database against the current row value, with the row locked while it runs. Read-modify-write in the app loses updates, and wrapping it in a transaction at read committed doesn't change that.

concepts.title: Read committed (Postgres default)
concepts.summary: Each statement sees data committed before it began, so two reads in one transaction can differ

variants.q: In a Postgres transaction at the default isolation level, you run the same `SELECT` twice and get different results, because another transaction committed in between. What's going on?
choices: Repeatable read: this should never be possible
Serializable: allowed, but only for `SELECT`
Read uncommitted: you're seeing uncommitted rows
Read committed: a new snapshot per statement
variants.explain: Postgres defaults to read committed, where every statement sees what was committed when it started. Postgres never shows uncommitted data, even if you ask for read uncommitted.

variants.q: A report runs several `SELECT`s in one Postgres transaction, and they must all see the same snapshot. What do you set?
choices: `ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ` on the transaction
`FOR SHARE` on the first `SELECT` only
Nothing: a transaction always uses one snapshot
A shorter `statement_timeout` for the report
variants.explain: Under repeatable read, the snapshot is taken at the first statement and kept for the whole transaction. At the default level, each statement gets its own.

concepts.title: Write skew
concepts.summary: Two transactions read the same data, then update different rows, breaking an invariant together

variants.q: At least one doctor must be on call. Alice and Bob both are. In two concurrent Postgres transactions at `REPEATABLE READ`, each checks 'is someone else on call?' (yes), then takes themself off. Both commit. What is this, and what prevents it?
choices: A dirty read; `READ COMMITTED` prevents it
Write skew; `SERIALIZABLE` prevents it
A lost update; `REPEATABLE READ` prevents it
A phantom read; a unique index prevents it
variants.explain: They updated different rows, so there's no write conflict to catch, yet together they broke the rule. Postgres's serializable level detects the dependency and aborts one.

variants.q: A customer has a checking row and a savings row. Either may go negative, but their combined balance must stay ≥ 0. Two Postgres transactions at `REPEATABLE READ` each read both rows (total 100), then withdraw 100: one from checking, one from savings. Both commit. What change makes Postgres abort one of them?
choices: A unique index on `(customer_id, kind)`
`READ COMMITTED` instead of `REPEATABLE READ`
`SERIALIZABLE`, retrying the one that fails
`FOR UPDATE` on only the row each one debits
variants.explain: Each transaction writes a different row, so there's no write conflict, and the rule lives in what both read. Serializable isolation tracks those read/write dependencies and aborts one; locking only the row you debit doesn't touch the row the other one changes.

concepts.title: Optimistic locking
concepts.summary: Detecting concurrent edits with a version column instead of holding locks

variants.q:
The document exists, but this update reports 0 rows affected. What does that mean?

```sql
UPDATE documents
SET body = $1, version = version + 1
WHERE id = $2 AND version = $3;
```
choices: Another transaction holds a lock on the row
The new body is identical to the old one
`version` overflowed and wrapped around
It changed since you read version `$3`
variants.explain: The `version` condition fails when another writer bumped it first, so your write is rejected instead of overwriting theirs. The app reloads and retries, or shows a conflict.

variants.q: Compared with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, when is a version column the better fit?
choices: Conflicts are rare; edits span think-time
Conflicts are frequent on one hot row
Writers must queue up in arrival order
The row must stay locked across many statements
variants.explain: Optimistic locking holds nothing while a user has a form open for minutes; it only checks at save time. With frequent conflicts, many saves fail and retry, and a lock is cheaper.

concepts.title: Transactional outbox
concepts.summary: Writing an event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the data, then publishing it

variants.q:
What's the risk if the process crashes between the commit and `publish`?

```ts
await db.tx(async (t) => {
  await t.none('INSERT INTO orders ...', order)
})
await broker.publish('order.created', order)
```
choices: The order is rolled back because the publish failed
The order exists, but `order.created` is never sent
The broker publishes the event twice after restart
Nothing: the broker buffers the publish until restart
variants.explain: The database and broker are two systems with no shared transaction, so a crash between them leaves one half done. An outbox row written in the same transaction makes the event as durable as the order.

variants.q: In the transactional outbox pattern, what's written in the same transaction as the business change?
choices: A lock that stops other services reading the new row
The broker offset, so the publish can be replayed later
A row describing the event, published later by a relay
A copy of the row in every consuming service's database
variants.explain: A relay (a poller or change data capture) publishes outbox rows after commit. It can publish a row twice if it crashes before marking it sent, so consumers still need to be idempotent.

variants.q: A relay publishes outbox rows to a broker, then marks each row as sent. It crashes after publishing a row but before marking it. What do consumers see after the restart?
choices: The same event twice, so they must handle duplicates
No event, because the unmarked row is skipped
The event once, because the broker de-duplicates
The event once, since the relay's marking is retried in the same transaction as the publish
variants.explain: The broker and the outbox table can't commit together, so the relay can only promise at-least-once publishing. Consumers need idempotent handling, such as ignoring an event id they've already processed.

concepts.title: Read-your-writes consistency
concepts.summary: Guaranteeing users see their own changes even when reads go to lagging replicas

variants.q: A user saves their profile (written to the primary). The page reloads, and the read goes to a replica 2 s behind, showing the old profile. Which guarantee is missing?
choices: Monotonic reads
Atomicity
Snapshot isolation
Read-your-writes
variants.explain: The user can't see a write they just made. Monotonic reads is a different promise: never seeing data go backwards across successive reads.

variants.q: What's a common way to provide read-your-writes on top of asynchronous replicas?
choices: Route a user's reads to the primary briefly after they write
Give the replicas bigger caches so they replay faster
Send writes to a replica first, then copy them to the primary
Put a longer TTL on cached copies of the profile page
variants.explain: Sticky routing after a write covers the user who wrote, while everyone else keeps reading cheap replicas. Waiting for a replica to pass the write's WAL position is a more precise variant.

concepts.title: Atomicity
concepts.summary: All statements in a transaction take effect together, or none of them do

variants.q: A transfer runs `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1`, then the matching `+ 100` for id 2, as two separate autocommit statements. The process crashes between them. What's the state, and what prevents it?
choices: Both updates are lost; just retry the transfer
Account 1 is debited but 2 isn't; use one transaction
The first update is rolled back automatically
Account 2 is credited twice; add a unique key
variants.explain: Each autocommit statement is its own transaction, so the first one is already durable when the crash happens. Putting both in one transaction makes them commit together or not at all.

variants.q: Inside `BEGIN`, an `INSERT` succeeds, then an `UPDATE` violates a constraint, and the code runs `ROLLBACK`. What happens to the inserted row?
choices: It stays, since it succeeded before the error
It stays, but is hidden until the next commit
It's removed only if the table has a foreign key
It's removed, with everything else in the transaction
variants.explain: `ROLLBACK` undoes every change made since `BEGIN`, whether or not that statement succeeded on its own. That's what lets a multi-step change fail cleanly.

skills.title: Migrations
skills.summary: Changing a live schema safely, backward compatible and reversible

concepts.title: Expand and contract
concepts.summary: Changing a schema in backward-compatible steps so old and new code can run at the same time

variants.q: You need to rename `users.fullname` to `users.display_name` with no downtime, while old and new app versions run side by side during a rolling deploy. Which order works?
choices: Rename the column in one migration, then deploy the new code
Add new column, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, drop old
Deploy code that reads `display_name`, then rename the column
Drop `fullname`, add `display_name`, and backfill from a backup
variants.explain: Each step keeps both app versions working: expand the schema, migrate the data and code, then contract once nothing uses the old column.

variants.q: Why can't you just run `ALTER TABLE users RENAME COLUMN fullname TO display_name` during a rolling deploy?
choices: Postgres can't rename a column with an index
A rename rewrites every row in the table
Old instances still query `fullname` and fail
Renames are blocked while replicas are connected
variants.explain: The rename itself is a quick catalog change; the problem is the old code still running. Any instance that hasn't been replaced breaks the moment the column changes name.

concepts.title: Adding a column with a default
concepts.summary: On Postgres 11+, a constant default is stored in the catalog; a volatile one rewrites the table

variants.q: On Postgres 11 or later, you run `ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN source text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'web'` on a 200-million-row table. How long does it hold its lock?
choices: Hours: every row is rewritten with the value
It fails: `NOT NULL` columns can't have defaults
Minutes: it backfills rows in batches by itself
Briefly: the default is stored in the catalog
variants.explain: Since Postgres 11, a non-volatile default is recorded once and returned for old rows on read, so no rewrite happens. The lock is still `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, just short (if it can get it quickly).

variants.q: On Postgres 13+, which `ADD COLUMN` forces a full table rewrite?
choices: `ADD COLUMN token uuid DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()`
`ADD COLUMN note text`
`ADD COLUMN status text DEFAULT 'new'`
`ADD COLUMN starts_at timestamptz DEFAULT '2026-01-01'`
variants.explain: `gen_random_uuid()` is volatile, so each row needs its own value and every row is written. Non-volatile defaults (and no default) are catalog-only changes.

concepts.title: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
concepts.summary: Building a Postgres index without blocking writes, at the cost of a slower build and some restrictions

variants.q: On a busy Postgres table, what does a plain `CREATE INDEX` (without `CONCURRENTLY`) block while it builds?
choices: Both reads and writes, throughout
Writes: inserts, updates, deletes
Nothing: index builds take no locks
Only reads that would use the index
variants.explain: A plain build takes a lock that allows reads but blocks writes until it finishes, which can be minutes on a big table. `CONCURRENTLY` lets writes continue.

variants.q: Your migration tool wraps every migration in a transaction. A migration runs `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`. What happens?
choices: It works, but holds its lock until the commit
Postgres silently builds it non-concurrently
It errors: not allowed in a transaction block
It works only if the table is currently empty
variants.explain: A concurrent build needs several transactions of its own, so Postgres refuses it inside one. Mark that migration as non-transactional; if a concurrent build fails, it leaves an `INVALID` index to drop.

concepts.title: Lock queues and lock_timeout
concepts.summary: A DDL statement waiting for a lock blocks every query queued behind it; `lock_timeout` limits the wait

variants.q: A migration runs `ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note text`, which needs an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock. A long analytics query is reading `orders`. Within seconds, every query on `orders` is stuck. Why?
choices: The `ALTER` is rewriting the whole table while holding its lock
The analytics query upgraded its own lock to exclusive
Postgres pauses every query during any schema change
The `ALTER` waits on the reader; new queries queue behind it
variants.explain: Lock requests queue in order, so new reads wait behind the pending exclusive lock even though they don't conflict with the analytics query. The change itself would take milliseconds.

variants.q: What's the usual protection when running schema changes like that on a busy database?
choices: A short `lock_timeout`, then retry the `ALTER`
A long `statement_timeout` so the `ALTER` can finish
Running the `ALTER` at `SERIALIZABLE` isolation
Running `VACUUM FULL` on the table beforehand
variants.explain: If the lock isn't granted quickly, the `ALTER` gives up and stops blocking the queue; you retry later. A long timeout makes the pile-up last longer.

concepts.title: Batched backfills
concepts.summary: Updating large tables in small committed batches instead of one giant statement

variants.q: You need to fill a new column on 80 million rows. Why not run one `UPDATE big_table SET col = ...`?
choices: Postgres caps a single `UPDATE` at 1 million rows
One huge transaction: long locks, bloat, lag
Postgres rejects an `UPDATE` with no `WHERE` clause
The new column isn't writable until after a restart
variants.explain: Every updated row stays locked until the end, every row gets a new version (bloat), and the WAL burst slows replicas. A failure at row 79 million rolls back everything.

variants.q: Which backfill approach is usually safest on a live table?
choices: One `UPDATE` at night, when traffic is at its lowest
One `UPDATE` inside a `SERIALIZABLE` transaction
Small batches by key range, each committed
One `UPDATE` with the table set to `UNLOGGED` first
variants.explain: Short batches hold locks briefly, let vacuum and replicas keep up, and can be paused or resumed. A night-time single update has the same problems, just with fewer witnesses.

concepts.title: Versioned migrations
concepts.summary: Schema changes kept as ordered files that a tool applies once each and records in the database

variants.q: A migration that already ran in production created a column named `adress`. What's the right fix?
choices: Edit the old migration file to say `address`
Rename the column in production by hand only
Add a new migration that renames the column
Delete the migration and recreate the table
variants.explain: The tool has recorded the old migration as applied and won't run it again, so editing it leaves environments out of sync (and tools that store checksums will refuse to continue). A new migration moves every environment forward the same way.

variants.q: How does a migration tool such as Flyway, golang-migrate or Alembic decide which migrations to run on deploy?
choices: It records applied versions in a table and runs the rest
It runs every migration file again on each deploy
It diffs the live schema against the code's models
It reads the latest git commit to find new files
variants.explain: Each tool keeps a table in the database (for example `flyway_schema_history`, `schema_migrations`, `alembic_version`) that says how far the schema has got, and applies only what comes after. Generating migrations from model diffs is a development-time step in some tools, not what runs on deploy.

skills.title: Relational vs NoSQL
skills.summary: How relational and NoSQL databases differ, and choosing one

concepts.title: CAP theorem
concepts.summary: During a network partition, a replicated system must choose between consistency and availability

variants.q: Two replicas lose contact with each other. A client asks one of them for a value that may have changed on the other side. Under CAP, what are its options?
choices: Answer fresh data by waiting for the other replica
Ignore the partition, since P is an optional property
Merge both sides' data and return the newest value
Answer possibly stale (A), or refuse until healed (C)
variants.explain: It can't reach the other side, so it either answers with what it has or declines. Waiting for the other replica is the 'refuse' option in disguise while the link is down.

variants.q: A vendor calls its distributed database 'CA: consistent and available, without partition tolerance'. What's wrong with that claim?
choices: Networks partition anyway, so P isn't optional
CA systems exist, but only for read-only data
CAP applies only to NoSQL, not to SQL systems
Partition tolerance is a speed feature, not a guarantee
variants.explain: Partitions happen whether or not you designed for them; the real question is what the system does when one occurs.

concepts.title: PACELC
concepts.summary: Extends CAP: when there's no partition, the trade-off is latency vs consistency

variants.q: There's no partition. Writes commit on the primary and replicas copy them asynchronously. In PACELC terms, which trade-off is this?
choices: Availability over consistency (PA)
Latency over consistency (EL)
Consistency over latency (EC)
Consistency over availability (PC)
variants.explain: With no partition, 'E' applies. Async replication answers fast and lets replicas lag, so it picks latency. PA/PC describe behaviour during a partition.

variants.q: You switch to synchronous replication: commits wait until a replica has applied the write. With no partition, what changes?
choices: Writes get faster; replica reads may now be stale
Partitions are tolerated with no trade-off at all
Replica reads are up to date; each write takes longer
Replica reads are up to date; writes are unaffected
variants.explain: Waiting for the replica buys consistency (EC) and costs a round trip on every write. It doesn't change what happens during a partition.

concepts.title: Access-pattern-first modeling
concepts.summary: In key-value stores like DynamoDB, designing keys around known queries instead of normalising entities

variants.q: You're designing a DynamoDB table. What's the recommended first step?
choices: Normalise into entities, then add indexes as queries appear
Copy the relational schema, one table per entity
Choose a partition key with few distinct values
List the access patterns, then design keys for them
variants.explain: DynamoDB serves queries efficiently only through keys and indexes built for them, so you start from the queries. Normalising first is the relational approach, which relies on joins DynamoDB doesn't have.

variants.q: In a relational database you can add a new kind of query later with an index. Why is that harder in DynamoDB?
choices: Queries need a key or index made for them
DynamoDB doesn't allow new indexes after table creation
Each new index doubles the table's storage bill
DynamoDB has no way to filter items at all
variants.explain: Without joins or a general query planner, a new access pattern usually means a new key design or a new GSI. GSIs can be added later; local secondary indexes can't.

concepts.title: Hot partition
concepts.summary: A partition key that concentrates traffic on one partition, throttling it while the rest sit idle

variants.q: A DynamoDB events table uses the event date (`2026-11-03`) as its partition key. Writes are throttled though total capacity is far from used. Why?
choices: DynamoDB can't hash date strings evenly
Today's writes all hit one key and its limit
The table needs a sort key before it accepts writes
A partition key can only be written from one client at a time
variants.explain: Throughput is spread by partition key, and each partition has a ceiling. When one key gets all the traffic, that ceiling is hit while the table's total capacity goes unused.

variants.q: An orders table serves 10,000 shops. Which partition key spreads write load most evenly?
choices: `country`
`status`
`order_id`
`created_date`
variants.explain: Order ids have many distinct, evenly used values. Country, status and date have few values, and the busiest ones become hot.

concepts.title: Indexing JSONB
concepts.summary: Which Postgres indexes help which `jsonb` queries: GIN for containment, expression B-trees for one field

variants.q: `events.data` is a `jsonb` column with a GIN index (default `jsonb_ops`). Which query can use that index?
choices: `WHERE data->>'type' = 'signup'`
`WHERE data @> '{"type": "signup"}'`
`WHERE (data->>'amount')::int > 100`
`WHERE data::text LIKE '%signup%'`
variants.explain: The default GIN operator class supports containment (`@>`) and key-existence operators. Extracting a field with `->>` produces a text value the GIN index doesn't cover.

variants.q: Your hot query is `WHERE data->>'customer_id' = $1` on a `jsonb` column. Which index fits it?
choices: A GIN index on the whole `data` column
A hash index on the whole `data` column
A B-tree on `(data->>'customer_id')`
None: `jsonb` fields can't be indexed
variants.explain: An expression index stores exactly the extracted value the query compares. A GIN index on `data` serves `@>` lookups, not `->>` equality.

concepts.title: Relational vs document databases
concepts.summary: Tables with joins and an enforced schema vs self-contained JSON documents, and which data fits each

variants.q: An order system has customers, orders, line items, products and inventory, with many cross-references and multi-row updates that must succeed together. Which default fits best?
choices: A document store with one document per customer
A relational database
A key-value cache
A time-series database
variants.explain: Many relationships, joins in both directions and multi-row transactions are what relational databases are built for. One document per customer makes queries across customers, such as 'all orders for product X', awkward and duplicates product data.

variants.q: A document database is described as 'schemaless'. What does that mean for your application in practice?
choices: Documents have no structure, so no validation is needed
The database infers a schema from the first document
The schema lives in your code, not in the database
Every field is stored as a string, so types don't matter
variants.explain: Your data still has a shape; by default the database just doesn't enforce it, so readers and writers in your code must agree on it and cope with older document versions.

concepts.title: Key-value stores
concepts.summary: Very fast reads and writes by exact key, but no filtering, joins or queries on other fields unless you build an index yourself

variants.q: Users are stored in a key-value store, keyed by `user_id`. Product now wants a page listing every user who signed up last week. What's the catch?
choices: Each value can hold only one field, not a whole user
Lookups go by key, so this needs a scan or an extra index
Dates can't be stored as values in a key-value store
The query works, but results come back in random order
variants.explain: A key-value store answers 'give me the value for this key' and little else, so a query on another field means scanning everything or maintaining a second key (an index) yourself. The value can be a whole JSON user; the limit is how you can find it.

variants.q: Which workload fits a key-value store best?
choices: Ad-hoc reports joining orders, customers and products
Finding every order over $100 placed in March
Making sure each order points at an existing customer
Loading a session by its session id on every request
variants.explain: Fetching one item by a known key is exactly what key-value stores are fast at. Joins, range filters on non-key fields and foreign keys are relational strengths.

skills.title: DB integration
skills.summary: Using a database from code: ORMs, connection pools and the N+1 problem

concepts.title: N+1 query
concepts.summary: Running one query for a list, then one more per item, instead of loading them together

choices: 51: the N+1 query problem
2: the driver batches the loop
1: `pg` joins the queries
50: a cartesian product
variants.explain: One query for the list plus one per row. Load all the customers at once with `WHERE id = ANY($1)` or a join.

variants.q:
What's the usual fix?

```go
posts, _ := store.ListPosts(ctx, 20) // 1 query
for i := range posts {
    posts[i].Author, _ = store.GetUser(ctx, posts[i].AuthorID) // 1 query each
}
```
choices: Run the `GetUser` calls in parallel goroutines
Load all authors at once with `WHERE id = ANY($1)`
Add an index on `users.id` to speed up each lookup
Raise the connection pool size so calls don't wait
variants.explain: One query for all the ids removes 20 round trips. Running them in parallel hides the latency but still sends 21 queries and takes 21 connections' worth of work.

variants.q:
What's the usual fix?

```python
posts = await store.list_posts(limit=20)  # 1 query
for post in posts:
    post.author = await store.get_user(post.author_id)  # 1 query each
```
choices: Wrap the loop in `asyncio.gather` so lookups run at once
Add an index on `users.id` to speed up each lookup
Load all authors in one query with `WHERE id = ANY(%s)`
Raise the connection pool size so calls don't wait
variants.explain: Fetching every author in one query replaces 20 round trips with one. `gather` overlaps them but still sends 21 queries.

variants.q: A blog page lists 30 posts with each post's comment count. The query log shows 31 queries per page view. What's the usual fix?
choices: Fetch all 30 counts in one grouped query
Add an index on `comments.post_id`
Run the 30 count queries in parallel
Cache each count in memory per request
variants.explain: One query for the list plus one per post is the N+1 shape, and it goes away by fetching all the counts together. An index makes each query cheaper, and parallelism overlaps them, but both still send 31 queries.

concepts.title: Connection pool sizing
concepts.summary: Pools across all app instances add up, and their total must fit the database's connection limit

variants.q: Postgres has `max_connections = 100`. You run 12 app pods, each with a pool of up to 20 connections. What happens at peak?
choices: Postgres queues the extra connections until some close
Each pod is limited to 100 ÷ 12 connections automatically
Nothing: idle connections don't count toward the limit
New ones past the limit are refused; pools want 240
variants.explain: The limit is global and every open connection counts, idle or not (a few slots are also reserved for superusers). Size pools so instances × pool size fits, or put a pooler like PgBouncer in front.

variants.q: A Go service uses `database/sql` and never calls `db.SetMaxOpenConns`. Under a traffic spike, what limits its open connections?
choices: Nothing: the default is unlimited
A default of 10 open connections per `*sql.DB`
`GOMAXPROCS`: one connection per OS thread
A default of 2 open connections from the driver
variants.explain: `MaxOpenConns` defaults to 0, meaning no limit, so a spike can open connections until the database refuses them. The 2 you may remember is the default number of idle connections kept.

variants.q: Postgres is at 100% CPU and requests wait for a free pooled connection. Someone triples every pod's pool size. What's the likely result?
choices: Throughput roughly triples, because requests no longer wait
More queries run at once on the same database, so latency stays the same or gets worse
CPU drops, because work is spread over more connections
The database queues the extra queries more efficiently than the app does
variants.explain: A bigger pool doesn't add database capacity; it lets more queries compete for the same CPU. Waiting for a connection in the app is often cheaper than contention inside the database.

concepts.title: Returning connections to the pool
concepts.summary: Every path, including errors and early returns, must give its connection back

choices: `rows.Err()` must be checked before the loop starts
Early returns leave `rows` open
`QueryContext` opens a brand-new pool on each call
`Scan` into an `int64` leaks a little memory per row
variants.explain: `rows` closes itself only when `Next` returns false (no more rows, or an error) or its context is cancelled. Each early return keeps a connection checked out, so the pool drains; add `defer rows.Close()` right after the error check.

choices: `pool.connect()` may only be called at startup
Each query needs `client.end()` afterwards
A throw skips `release()`
The pool grows beyond `max` and then blocks
variants.explain: Each `NotFound` (and any query error) leaks one client. Once all are leaked, `connect()` waits forever. `pool.query` handles checkout and release for single queries.

variants.q:
(psycopg_pool) After a while, every request blocks on `getconn()` until it times out. Why?

```python
conn = pool.getconn()
row = conn.execute("SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE id = %s", (job_id,)).fetchone()
if row is None:
    raise NotFound(job_id)
pool.putconn(conn)
return row
```
choices: `getconn` may only be called once per process
Each query needs `conn.close()` after it
The pool grows beyond `max_size` and blocks
A raise skips `putconn`
variants.explain: Every `NotFound` leaks a connection until the pool is empty. The `with pool.connection()` context manager returns it on every path, exceptions included.

variants.q: A function checks out a database connection and runs a query. Which structure makes sure the connection goes back to the pool on every path?
choices: Release it on the last line of the function body
Release it in the error handler only, not on success
Rely on the pool's idle timeout to reclaim leaked connections
Release it in a `finally` / `defer` / context manager
variants.explain: Cleanup tied to the acquisition runs on early returns and exceptions too. A release on the last line is skipped by any early exit, and idle timeouts don't reclaim a connection that's checked out.

concepts.title: Using the transaction's connection
concepts.summary: Statements meant for a transaction must go through its handle or connection, not the pool

choices: The `UPDATE` uses `db`, so it runs outside the transaction
`defer tx.Rollback()` undoes the commit when the function ends
`BeginTx` with `nil` options doesn't start a transaction
Two statements in one transaction need `SERIALIZABLE`
variants.explain: `db` takes another connection from the pool, so the `UPDATE` commits on its own and isn't undone if the transaction rolls back. `Rollback` after a successful `Commit` is a harmless no-op.

variants.q:
(node-postgres `Pool`) Why isn't this a reliable transaction?

```ts
await pool.query('BEGIN')
await pool.query('INSERT INTO orders ...')
await pool.query('UPDATE stock ...')
await pool.query('COMMIT')
```
choices: `BEGIN` must be part of the first statement's text
Each `pool.query` may use a different connection
node-postgres doesn't support transactions
`COMMIT` has to be sent before the `UPDATE`
variants.explain: A transaction lives on one connection. Check out a client with `pool.connect()`, run all four statements on it, then release it.

variants.q: `placeOrder` calls `orderRepo.insert(order)` and `stockRepo.decrement(item)`, and each repository takes its own connection from the pool. It must be all-or-nothing. What's needed?
choices: Pass one transaction handle into both repository calls
Call a rollback method on each repository if the other fails
Run both calls in parallel threads to shorten the window
Use `SERIALIZABLE` on each repository's connection
variants.explain: Atomicity needs both statements on the same connection inside one transaction. Separate connections commit separately, and an isolation level doesn't join them.

variants.q:
In `psycopg_pool`, what happens to the stock update if the outer transaction rolls back after `reserve_stock` returns?

```python
def reserve_stock(item_id: int) -> None:
    with pool.connection() as conn:
        conn.execute("UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE id = %s", (item_id,))

with pool.connection() as conn:
    with conn.transaction():
        conn.execute("INSERT INTO orders ...")
        reserve_stock(item_id)
        raise PaymentDeclined()
```
choices: It's rolled back, because it ran in the same process
It's rolled back, because `pool.connection()` joins the open transaction
It stays committed: it ran on a different connection
It's never committed, because `reserve_stock` doesn't call `commit()`
variants.explain: `pool.connection()` hands out a separate connection, and leaving its `with` block commits. The outer rollback only covers statements on the outer connection.

concepts.title: Network calls inside transactions
concepts.summary: Holding a transaction open across an HTTP call keeps its locks and connection busy for the whole call

choices: The HTTP charge is rolled back if the transaction fails
`FOR UPDATE` is ignored when used inside `db.tx`
The lock and connection are held during the HTTP call
The transaction times out after 200 ms by default
variants.explain: Slow calls pin a connection and a row lock each, so the pool drains and other writers queue. And if the transaction fails afterwards, the charge isn't rolled back: the card is charged with no record.

variants.q: Which structure is usually better for 'charge the card, then record the charge'?
choices: Open the transaction earlier so it also covers the API call
Raise the pool size so slow calls don't starve the others
Use `SERIALIZABLE` so the API call becomes part of the commit
Commit a pending row, call the API, then record the result
variants.explain: The pending row records intent durably, the external call holds no database resources, and a later step (or a reconciler) records the outcome. No isolation level can make an HTTP call atomic with a commit.

variants.q: A handler opens a transaction, inserts an order row, calls a shipping provider's API (usually 300 ms, sometimes 20 s), then updates the row and commits. Under load, which symptom appears first?
choices: Duplicate key errors on the order row when it is retried
Pool exhaustion and lock waits while slow calls hold resources
Phantom reads for other concurrent readers of the table
Replication lag on every read replica in the cluster
variants.explain: The transaction holds a connection (and any locks it took) for the whole API call, so slow responses pin pool slots and make other writers wait. The other symptoms aren't caused by the call's duration.

concepts.title: PgBouncer transaction pooling
concepts.summary: In transaction mode each transaction may get a different server connection, so session state can't be relied on

variants.q: Through PgBouncer in **transaction** pooling mode, a worker calls `SELECT pg_advisory_lock(42)` in one transaction and `pg_advisory_unlock(42)` in a later one. What can go wrong?
choices: The unlock may run on another connection; the lock stays held
PgBouncer quietly turns session advisory locks into row-level locks
The lock is released automatically at the end of the first transaction
Advisory locks are cluster-wide, so PgBouncer serialises every client
variants.explain: A session-level advisory lock belongs to the server connection, and the next transaction may get a different one. Use `pg_advisory_xact_lock`, which is released at commit.

variants.q: With PgBouncer in transaction mode, which kind of state is safe to rely on?
choices: A `LISTEN` registered once when the app starts up
Transaction-scoped state, like `SET LOCAL`
A session-level `SET` sent once on connect
A temp table created at the start of the session
variants.explain: Only state scoped to the transaction is guaranteed to be on the same server connection. Session state may sit on a connection another client gets next, or be missing from yours.
